text.p: Wik and Hansen
By Russell Barton (ABC TV Political Editor)
The Howard government has moved into the uncomfortable mid-term phase and is discovering its hard yards from here to the next election.

In contrast to the first 12 months, when the government could initiate policy direction, John Howard finds himself now in reactive mode, facing each morning with a desk-full of problems requiring urgent attention.
None is more urgent than Wik.
The longer Howard dallies over the land wrangle, the bolder become his opponents on both sides of the debate.
The Aborigines have fallen, once again, to threatening the Olympics.
More immediate is their threat to take Howard's 10-point plan to the High Court.
Some certainty that will be.
And yet the 10-point plan does not go far enough for his own coalition colleagues.

Howard yesterday outlined to his backbench committee the tortuous path to title certainty he has devised, by adopting the Income Tax Act's definition of rural activities which can be pursued on pastoral leases while at the same time severely limiting Aborigines' rights under co-existing native title.
One of the prime minister's strongest arguments in favour of his approach -- apart from the warning that anything else will end up back in the High Court -- is the compensation question.
Extinguishment would create prospective compensation worth billions of dollars.
And that managed to turn the committee.
Most of those breathing fire and brimstone on their way into the meeting came out talking more constructively, prepared to wait for more detail.
The committee is an important conduit to the backbench and it seems Howard has secured its eventual support.

But his plan is still not enough to convince the entire backbench, particularly the Queenslanders who are under immense pressure from constituents already "wikked off" over other perceived incursions such as gun control.
While this painful process is not over, in the end Howard can probably count on the Labor Party, of all people, to help him to resolution.
Kim Beazley's seven-point plan is not far from Howard's approach.
When that becomes publicly evident, the Queensland Nationals will find themselves isolated in the parliament.
But that doesn't mean their constituents will be satisfied.
The sudden burst of popularity for Pauline Hanson carries a cautionary tale.
Forget the AGB McNair poll suggesting up to 25 percent might consider voting for her One Nation party; the question was so sloppily framed it could mean anything.
But the government is taking more seriously the Morgan poll's finding of 10 percent nationwide support -- 20 percent in Queensland.
That's been extrapolated by the Australian Democrats to produce three Senate seats for Pauline Hanson.

Howard says Hanson will wither on the vine before the next election, that the electorate will eventually demand from her realistic solutions to the now familiar list of problems she raises -- native title, foreign investment, immigration and, of course, unemployment.
It's this last issue which is the most damaging for Howard over the long-term.
Stuck on 8.7 percent, the jobless rate will not improve in the medium term and it may not even hit the financial year-end target of 8.5 percent on time.
Howard himself can offer no hope.
Consider these extracts of his response to Hanson in his 3AW interview this week: "I mean I sympathise with people who feel uneasy and insecure..."
"Now it's easy to finger the act that people feel uneasy and unhappy..."

"...I would counsel all of my colleagues on the Liberal and National Party side of politics to remember the passing phenomena of earlier years, to remember the transient appeal of the populist who pretends to articulate the concerns but has none of the answers. They've come and gone in the past and I believe that will be the case with this particular phenomenom."
That failed to calm the colleagues.
The next day, Foreign Minister Alexander Downer came out with his strongest speech yet on the impact of Hanson.
"The views of Pauline Hanson if they were ever to become official Australian policy would not cost a few jobs; they would cost Australia tens of thousands of jobs."
And Tim Fischer at his mysterious best: "We choose our moments to put a counter viewpoint .. you've seen nothing yet compared to what is coming."
What is coming from Howard is a lofty silence.
That would be a sound strategy if, at the same time, he was coming up with answers himself.
But there's been nothing on unemployment likely to deliver the "comfortable and relaxed" mood he promised the electorate before the last election.
Indeed, faced with BHP's announcement of the impending shutdown of the Newcastle steelworks, Howard could offer nothing but tea and sympathy.
"Look, I don't pretend for a moment and nobody should pretend that governments can intervene and reverse commercial decisions of that kind."
In the absence of an improvement in employment, Howard must develop a more positive political strategy to deal with the jobs issue than that.
Leadership it's not.
-- Reuters Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
